{{Short description|American physicist}}
'''Yuri Kovchegov''' (born 1973) is an American [[physicist]].

==Biography==
Kovchegov obtained his bachelor's degree from the [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]] in 1993 and two years later got his master's from [[Columbia University]] following by Ph.D. in 1998 at the same place. From 1998 to 1999 he worked at the [[University of Minnesota]] as a postdoc and then became theoretical research associate at [[Brookhaven National Laboratory]]. From 2000 to 2004 he served as a research assistant professor at the [[University of Washington]] and then became [[Ohio State University]]'s assistant professor in 2004 following by a promotion there to the associate professor in 2008 and to the professor in 2012. In August 2001 he was awarded ''travel award'' from the [[National Science Foundation]] and on May 21, 2006 he was awarded ''Raymond and Beverly [[Sackler Prize]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.physics.ohio-state.edu/briefcvs/kovchegov_briefcv.pdf|title=Yuri Kovchegov|pages=1–2|access-date=December 25, 2013}}</ref> He is also a [[fellow]] at the [[American Physical Society]].<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.physics.ohio-state.edu/~yuri/|title=Yuri Kovchegov|access-date=December 25, 2013}}</ref>

==Research==
On September 28, 1998 he along with [[Alfred Mueller|A.H. Mueller]] used the formula <math> -\frac{1}{4}G^a_{\mu \nu} G^{\mu \nu}_a </math> to calculate the production of [[gluon]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|date=September 28, 1998|volume=529 |issue=1–2|author =Yuri V. Kovchegov and A.H. Mueller|title=Gluon production in current-nucleus and nucleon-nucleus collisions in a quasi-classical approximation|journal=[[Nuclear Physics B]]|pages=451–479|doi=10.1016/S0550-3213(98)00384-8|arxiv = hep-ph/9802440 |bibcode = 1998NuPhB.529..451K |s2cid=9526886 }}</ref>

==Writings==
* with Eugene Levin: Quantum Chromodynamics at High Energy. Cambridge University Press 2012.
